I'm writing this on the 31st of may 2025, rtx 5000 cards launched, scalpers are still an issue, prices are higher than ever before, nvidia is pulling tricks to deceive us into thinking that the entry level cards(aka the 5060/5060ti) are more performant than they actually are, and yet 1080ti buyers from that time still enjoy their games with medium-high settings, no ray tracing (like amd gpu users of yester year) and use upscaling tech from amd and intel because nvidia is trying to make this legendary card obsolete.
I own a RTX 4060Ti (8gb) and i am dissapointed by it, yet power efficiency and size constraints forced me this way... but if i were to go back in time and build a normal sized pc i would get a 1080ti for $200 instead of this 4060ti for $450, i would enjoy similar performance and would only lack ray tracing.
All in all the 1080TI is still a great option in 2025.

comments.text:
I'm well late with this comment (6 years!) but I'm just looking through the history of graphics cards. I'm thinking of getting back into gaming this year and it's been over 15 years since I really played a lot of PC games. Was born in '82, so I've seen such a huge evolution of computing and graphics.

It's interesting this year that AMD is adding GPU cores into it's CPUs that are, amazingly, good enough to run games at high! That's mind blowing. What would be incredible, is if your CPU/GPU combo chip (APU.. apparently) could combine or work in parallel with whatever graphics card you have installed. An automatic SLI with your CPU genuinely putting in extra effort. Maybe split the tasks between the slot-in GPU and the APU, like DLSS frame generation or ray tracing, anti-aliasing  - or one keeps the vertices and the main card covers them in textures. I dunno - this is probably impossible, but really interesting to think about now that CPUs are getting so ridiculously complicated in order to keep up with Moore's Law in terms of processing ability. So we've gone down the hyper threading route, down the multiple core route, now we've thrown in a graphics card into the CPU as well.. what would be amazing is if it combined with whatever you put into the machine and upgraded it by taking on some of its tasks.

I have a ridiculously maxed out PC, with everything as high end as possible - but with a real basic graphics card that is passively cooled and can handle 3 screens - because my job is music production, music related things.

This is one area that really annoys me - both Intel and AMD don't really optimise for music applications where ultra low latency (pressing a key - hearing that note) is essential. It's been done on some processors, that have become desirable for music producers for that very reason.. but its not guaranteed. Also, music production applications don't care about threading or cores, it needs a ridiculously high single thread score, as all the effects (EQ, reverb, compression.. you name it, whatever the effect is) put on the sound are moving through the digital audio workstation software and have to be done in order on a single thread. It can't split the sound up and get other threads to affect it, then recombine it at the end. That would be a logistical nightmare in terms of programming, I don't even think it could be done.

Ah... the last anomaly card. 

A mistake that Jenson will NEVER make again. Making a powerhouse product rather cheap. Mind you, $700 wasn't "cheap" then. But it's value for what you got is what made this card the icon it was and still is today, almost 7 years later. 

I get everyone loves using this card as the poster child for "the good ol days" but in reality. It was a fluke and not the norm even then. So the "good ol days" was never real outside this one release. Sure, there were actual cheap and somewhat competent GPU's too. But not like this. And everyone since this, has expected a repeat every generation. lol

I also think it's a hard pill for some to swallow.

+Generic Username
it's not that simple.

if the code does not call for more than 4 cores or threads, the rest will idle. and peak usage for that particular application will be 25% in a r7, since it's only using 1/4 of the total threads (even though total performance should be closer to 45%. SMT threads aren't even close to being as relevant as normal primary threads). that's why it shows 20-40% usage.

having more cores won't hurt you, but they don't always help either.

comments.text: You should get 6850k (40 pcie lanes) or a 7700k (16 pcie lanes) on a motherboard that has a PLX  switch (allows both cards to be connected in 16x mode even if the processor has only 16 lanes). For 4k you need to run your cards in 16x mode. I tested with 2 x 1080 in SLI with 4790k on two different motherboards, one with PLX and one without (16x vs 8x pcie) and there was a 10-15% difference throughout  multiple games. With 1080ti probably is a bigger difference. Ryzen only have 24 lane, so if there is no motherboard with plx switch for it is a big NO NO for SLI. comments.text:
For the current frame rate discussion:
Many will say we can't see past 30, others past 60, etc. Nothing has been essentially 'proved' true or false.
But there is one thing that will get all of them to agree: VR

If a game does not deliver FPS above a set limit, your body can and will simply get sick.
The brain loves information -- it doesn't always process it all, but it really hates it when vital info is missing.

While not everyone has tried VR nor experienced motion sickness, hopefully you have experienced an unoptimized game.
If you recall the weird hitching/judder and the feeling of being thrown off when it happened.
Think of that when folks tell you they can't play on anything below 60, or if others tell you they prefer/don't care for anything higher than 30.
Think the same when you get those that don't care/don't know what FPS is.

As gamers, we find and get used to whatever FPS we are most comfortable with -- let others find their ground and then show them the buttery smoothness that is 60 - come back a year or so later and show them 120...

Most single thread tests I have seen Intel wins, but where Ryzen is really shining is multi-thread tasks. Another thing Ryzen has been getting praise for is it's workstation performance e.g. Adobe CC apps, video editing, photo editing, etc. 

   Bottom line is this is a new kind of chip, that's introducing a whole new ball game to the market with features and cores that we haven't seen intel offer to consumers at a price everyone can afford. Ryzen will be a success, you just have to give it time, and there is a big market out there that wants the workstation grade performance and performance beyond 1080p, AMD realizes this, that's why they've made 8 cores/16 threads affordable. Hopefully we see game developers start using more cores, and we'll see increased performance there. Just like when 64-bit first came out, developers adapted quick. comments.text:
People aren't going to hold onto their old monitors forever. I for one aren't going to step up to 4k until the performance does rise higher with the best cards on the market, but I do want to see these results to see how the tech gradually rises to meet the challenge. Personally I don't care about 1080p, but many people do so they should test that, 2560x1440 and maybe even 3440x1440 ultrawide thrown in for good measure.

It's the same argument that's been had with Ryzen, just with the situation reversed. 4k results are valuable in showing a GPU stressed to its max. But the percentage of people gaming with a 700 dollar card on 4k is still less than the percentage gaming on 1080p with a 330-500 dollar cpus it seems. So those lower resolutions are even more important here for real world use cases than higher resolutions are as significant real world gaming cases for Ryzen.

TL;DR: Linus and crew have done a fine job I argue with the testing here, but I concede a more complete picture would be helpful to a number of people.

To be quite honest, the last three years is where manufacturing costs have gone down considerably, they were always expensive processes. 

Most of the CPU's over $1000 are that way because of niche usage, or because they are needed for more powerful tasks and have a lot of redundancies. 

Binning is also a factor here, in the manufacturing of a die, you have some which are going to be high end. and others which have to go lower. But this isn't controlled for the most part, there are points where you get less of a functional yield than you set out to obtain. 

The titans actually were great cards up until the Titan X and Titan XP, they were originally meant to be affordable workstation cards with the capability of gaming as a secondary. They were an expensive process. 

Then the name of "titan" fell out of grace and into a "gaming" title brand. And to be honest, it's more about having the best power for your buck early, people really want that, and it's not a bad thing as it helps establish an economy.

Silicon is cheap, yes, but the extremely refined, and pure version used in processors isn't cheap to refine for CPU's and GPUs of modern days. Each individual processor would be more along the lines of $24-50 depending on die size and process. Now that the sizes keep getting smaller, they can be put on the same sized dies but with less input. But the rate of loss is still consistent. 

Lower grade chips are going to use less pure ingots sure, but the process behind that is less strenuous compared to what goes into something like a modern GPU or CPU chip. It is the real definition of Software Bloat and Code Bloat, where programmers don't streamline or clean their code and just do a working mess because they trust that powerful hardware is capable of running it or will be capable in a short time. It is cheaper and faster to assume that hardware will do it "just fine" and these things happen, that we are never able to max out any new game with average hardware.
